passage:
Class 4 notes, Tanuja, class teacher
During morning assembly, Zeenat tripped on the step while carrying the attendance register to the stage. She didn't fall, only wobbled, and caught herself on the rail. Back in class she sat with her head down on her arms. At lunch she told me, "Everyone saw. They'll call me Wobbly till Class 10."
I asked her to look around. Bilal was hunting for his lost eraser, Gauri was worried about her spelling test, and two girls were arguing over whose turn it was on the swing. Nobody had mentioned the step.
Tomorrow I'll ask Zeenat to carry the register again, and I'll quietly tell her how I once dropped a whole box of chalk in front of the principal.

qa.q: What was Zeenat carrying when she tripped?
qa.a: She was carrying the attendance register to the stage.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Zeenat that everyone will call her Wobbly till Class 10?
qa.a: Zeenat feels so embarrassed that the wobble seems huge from the inside, and she imagines every eye was on her, even though the others were busy with erasers, spelling and the swing. 😰

qa.q: Why is Tanuja's plan to let Zeenat carry the register again a good choice?
qa.a: Doing it again soon lets Zeenat see that nobody remembers, which shrinks the fear before it grows.

qa.q: What was that assembly like for Gauri, who was worried about her spelling test?
qa.a: Gauri was probably so busy with her own worry that she never noticed the wobble at all.

grounding: A teacher notes a girl who wobbled at assembly sure everyone will remember, while classmates were busy with their own worries.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today in science Miss asked what plants breathe in, and I said OXYGEN, really loud. Wrong! It's carbon dioxide. I wanted to crawl under the bench. I was SURE everyone was laughing inside.
At break I told Keerthana, "The whole class will remember this forever."
She blinked. "When did you say that?"
She didn't even remember! She was busy thinking about her dance practice. Then Rehan asked me for a spare pencil like nothing had happened.
Maybe people don't keep a list of my mistakes. Maybe they keep lists of their own.
Still, I'm going to read the plant chapter twice. 😅
Ayesha

qa.q: What answer did Ayesha give in science?
qa.a: Ayesha said OXYGEN, really loud.

qa.q: Why was Ayesha so sure everyone was laughing inside?
qa.a: Ayesha felt so embarrassed that the mistake seemed enormous, and it felt obvious that the whole class had noticed and would keep it in mind.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha change her mind, and what could Ayesha try the next time a mistake feels huge?
qa.a: Asking Keerthana showed that nobody remembered; next time Ayesha could check with a friend before deciding everyone is laughing. 🙂

qa.q: What was that science lesson like for Keerthana?
qa.a: Keerthana was busy thinking about dance practice, so the wrong answer barely registered for her.

grounding: A child who gives a wrong answer is sure the class will remember, then finds Keerthana didn't even notice.

passage:
At the gurdwara sports day in their village near Moga, Jasleen tripped in the sack race and rolled right onto the chalk line. She got up with dust on her salwar and finished last. For the rest of the afternoon she stood behind a tent pole, sure the whole village was pointing at her.
"Everyone saw me fall," she whispered to Rajni.
Rajni was licking jalebi syrup off her fingers. "Fall when?"
Across the ground, the boys were arguing about the tug-of-war rope, the aunties were counting prize cups, and the sack-race winner was crying because his sack had torn.
Jasleen came out from behind the pole, just a little.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen stand for the rest of the afternoon?
qa.a: She stood behind a tent pole.

qa.q: Why does Jasleen believe the whole village was pointing at her?
qa.a: The fall felt so big to her that she assumed it was the biggest thing everyone else had seen too.

qa.q: What turning point brought Jasleen out from behind the pole?
qa.a: Rajni's "Fall when?" showed that even her friend hadn't noticed, and she could see everyone busy with their own things. 🙂

qa.q: How was the sack race for the winner, compared with how Jasleen saw it?
qa.a: The winner was busy crying over a torn sack, far too caught up to think about Jasleen's fall.

grounding: A village girl who fell in a race is sure everyone saw, while others were busy with their own troubles.

passage:
Dalia, nine, had one line in the school play in Amman: "The river is rising!" When the moment came, she said, "The rising is river!"
A few children giggled. Dalia's face burned all the way through the final song. At home she refused dinner. "Everyone heard. Everyone will remember forever. I'm never going back."
Her brother Siddiq, who had been in the same play as a tree, looked up from his plate. "What did you say wrong?"
"You were right there!"
"I was trying not to sneeze," Siddiq said. "My leaves were itchy."
The next morning at the school gate, Dalia's best friend ran up. "Did you see my crown fell off? I was so embarrassed!"
Dalia hadn't seen that at all.

qa.q: What did Dalia say instead of 'The river is rising!'?
qa.a: She said, "The rising is river!"

qa.q: How did Dalia feel after her mistake, and what shows it?
qa.a: Dalia felt deeply embarrassed; her face burned through the final song, she refused dinner and said everyone would remember forever.

qa.q: What could Dalia notice from Siddiq and her friend next time she makes a slip?
qa.a: She could remember that Siddiq didn't notice because of his itchy leaves and her friend was busy worrying about her crown, so most people are thinking about their own worries.

qa.q: How might Dalia's best friend have felt about the crown falling off?
qa.a: Her best friend felt embarrassed, just like Dalia, and probably thought everyone had seen the crown, even though Dalia hadn't noticed at all.

grounding: It shows a girl who fumbled her line believing everyone saw, while others were busy with their own worries.

passage:
At the swimming club in Chandigarh, the Saturday class lined up at the pool edge. Amandeep, ten, walked forward and slipped on the wet tiles, landing on his bottom with a loud slap. His face went red. He was sure the whole class had turned to look.
For the rest of the lesson he stayed at the far end of the pool, head down, and didn't try the dive even once. In the changing room he whispered to Jatin, "Everyone saw me fall. They'll call me Slippy for the whole year."
Jatin was fighting with his goggle strap. "You fell? When?"
"At the start! It was so loud!"
"I was looking for my other flip-flop," Jatin said. "Coach was shouting at Ishani about her cap."
Amandeep stood there with one sock on, thinking. Nobody else in the changing room was talking about it at all.

qa.q: What was Jatin doing in the changing room?
qa.a: Jatin was fighting with the goggle strap.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep stay at the far end of the pool for the rest of the lesson?
qa.a: He felt so embarrassed that he believed the whole class had seen him fall and would call him Slippy all year, so he tried to hide.

qa.q: What small step could Amandeep take at the next class?
qa.a: He could try the dive, remembering that Jatin didn't even see him fall and nobody in the changing room was talking about it.

qa.q: How did Jatin's afternoon look different from how Amandeep imagined it?
qa.a: Jatin was busy looking for a lost flip-flop and struggling with the goggle strap, so the fall went completely unseen.

grounding: It shows a boy who slipped at the pool believing everyone saw and would remember, while others were busy with their own concerns.

passage:
Friday
The worst day of my whole life. At the annual day rehearsal I tripped on the stage steps in front of EVERYONE. My shoe came off and rolled. I'm sure the whole school saw. They'll call me Shoe Girl until Class 10.
I didn't eat lunch. I sat in the library so nobody could laugh.
Then at home time Indu asked why I wasn't in the canteen. I said, "Because of the shoe!" She said, "What shoe?" SHE DIDN'T EVEN SEE. She was busy panicking about forgetting her own lines. Then Rafiya said she only noticed because her own dupatta was coming loose at the same time.
So maybe it wasn't everyone. Maybe it was like three people. Maybe nobody will remember by Monday.
Still. My face is hot just writing it.
Zainab

qa.q: What did Indu say when Zainab mentioned the shoe?
qa.a: "What shoe?"

qa.q: Why did Zainab sit in the library at lunch?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and sure the whole school had seen her trip, so she hid to avoid being laughed at.

qa.q: What could Zainab remember the next time she stumbles in front of others?
qa.a: That most people are busy with their own worries, like Indu with her lines, so far fewer notice or remember than it feels.

qa.q: What was Indu busy with during the rehearsal?
qa.a: Indu was panicking about forgetting her own lines, so she didn't even see the shoe.

grounding: A girl's diary shows being sure the whole school saw her trip, while her friends were busy with their own worries.

passage: At morning assembly in the village school, Mohit was chosen to read the day's thought from the notice board. He stepped up to the microphone, which crackled and squealed, and read "honesty is the best polish" instead of "policy." A few boys at the front giggled. Mohit's ears went red. All morning he kept his head down. At break he hid behind the water tank, sure the whole school, even the Class 8 boys and the headmaster, was still laughing. Darshan found him there. "Why are you hiding?" "Because of polish!" Darshan looked blank. "What polish? I was busy trying to remember if I brought my maths book." Mohit peeped out. The Class 8 boys were playing gilli-danda. Nobody even looked his way.

qa.q: What did Mohit read instead of "policy"?
qa.a: Polish.

qa.q: Why did Mohit hide behind the water tank?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and sure everyone, even the Class 8 boys and the headmaster, was still laughing at his mistake.

qa.q: What could help Mohit after a small mistake like this?
qa.a: Checking what others are really doing, like the boys playing gilli-danda, and remembering most people are thinking about their own things.

qa.q: Why didn't Darshan notice the mistake?
qa.a: Darshan was busy trying to remember whether he had brought his maths book.

grounding: A boy misreads one word at assembly and is sure the whole school is still laughing, while most never noticed.

passage: In Tuan's classroom in Hanoi, the teacher asked what seven times eight was, and Tuan, half asleep, said, "Fifty-four." Somebody snorted. The teacher said, "Fifty-six," and moved on. But Tuan's face burned for the rest of the lesson. That night he lay awake, replaying it. By tomorrow, he thought, the whole class will be calling me Fifty-Four. In the morning he walked in slowly, waiting for the jokes. Nothing. Aiko, who sat beside him, was complaining about her lost pencil case. At lunch Tuan finally asked her, "Did you hear what I said in maths yesterday?" Aiko frowned. "Yesterday? I was busy trying to finish my drawing before the bell." Tuan let out a long breath, and then laughed at himself.

qa.q: What was Tuan's wrong answer?
qa.a: Fifty-four.

qa.q: Why did Tuan lie awake that night?
qa.a: He felt anxious and embarrassed, sure the whole class would remember and call him Fifty-Four.

qa.q: What could Tuan tell himself the next time he makes a small mistake in class?
qa.a: That most classmates are busy with their own things, like Aiko with her drawing, so a small slip is quickly forgotten.

qa.q: What was on Aiko's mind the next morning?
qa.a: Aiko was complaining about her lost pencil case, not thinking about Tuan's answer at all.

grounding: A boy gives one wrong answer and is sure the class will remember, while his neighbour never even noticed.

passage: At the Monday assembly in the Indore school, Jagdish had to walk up the stage steps to receive the drawing prize. On the second step his foot slipped and he stumbled, catching himself on the railing. He got the certificate, walked back to his line and stared at his shoes, face burning. The whole school had seen. Four hundred children. They would laugh about it for the rest of the year. He didn't go to the canteen at break. At lunch, Noor sat down beside him. "Congratulations on the prize! Your drawing was the one with the elephant, na?" Jagdish mumbled, "Did you see me fall?" Noor looked blank. "You fell? When?" She had been worrying about her own speech in English class all through assembly.

qa.q: What prize did Jagdish receive at assembly?
qa.a: The drawing prize.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he stared at his shoes?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and sure the whole school had seen and would laugh at him for the rest of the year.

qa.q: What could Jagdish remember the next time he makes a small slip?
qa.a: That most people, like Noor, are busy with their own worries and barely notice or remember other people's small mistakes.

qa.q: What was Noor thinking about during assembly?
qa.a: Noor was worrying about her own speech in English class, so she never noticed Jagdish stumble.

grounding: Shows a child sure the whole school saw his stumble and will remember it, while a classmate never even noticed.

passage:
Tuesday. In science class, Keerthana answered that the moon makes its own light. Some children giggled. Her face went hot. For the rest of the day she was sure the whole class was whispering about her.
Wednesday. She didn't raise her hand once. She pretended to be sick at PT, so nobody would look at her. At home she told her mother everyone would call her "moon girl" forever.
Friday. In the art room, she asked Hrithik, very quietly, "Do you remember what I said about the moon?" Hrithik frowned and kept colouring. "What about the moon?" "On Tuesday. In science." He shrugged. "I don't remember. I was worried about my own homework." Keerthana stared at him. Two whole days of hiding, and he didn't even remember.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say about the moon in science class?
qa.a: She answered that the moon makes its own light.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and anxious, sure everyone would call her "moon girl" forever, so she hid from attention.

qa.q: What could Keerthana try next time she makes a mistake in class?
qa.a: She could remind herself that most classmates are busy with their own worries, and keep taking part instead of hiding.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik not remember the moon answer?
qa.a: He was worried about his own homework, so Keerthana's answer barely registered for him.

grounding: Shows over several days a child sure her wrong answer is remembered by the whole class, while a classmate has forgotten it.

passage: Manoj, you're hiding because you said the wrong answer in class? Come here, sit with your Indu Nani. When I was nine, in Mysore, I was in the Dasara dance programme at school. Right in the middle, my anklet came loose and I tripped. I didn't fall, only stumbled, but I was certain the whole town had seen. For a week I wouldn't go to school. Then my best friend came to our house. I asked her, "What did everyone say about my fall?" She said, "What fall?" She had been so busy worrying about her own steps that she saw nothing. I spent a week hiding for something nobody remembered. So, Manoj. Who do you think is still thinking about your answer?

qa.q: What came loose during young Indu's dance?
qa.a: Her anklet came loose.

qa.q: What was young Indu feeling during the week she stayed home?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and afraid, certain the whole town had seen her stumble and was talking about it.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed how young Indu saw her stumble?
qa.a: When her best friend said, "What fall?", showing she had been too busy worrying about her own steps to notice.

qa.q: How might the best friend have felt hearing Indu had hidden for a week?
qa.a: The friend was probably surprised and a little sad that Indu had suffered over something no one had noticed.

grounding: An elder recalls stumbling in a school dance and hiding for a week, sure everyone had seen, when her friend hadn't noticed at all.

passage:
On Republic Day the fog was so thick that the back rows of the assembly could barely see the stage. The microphone crackled in the cold, and Sir kept tapping it.
Lokesh, carrying the tray of paper flags, caught his shoe on the second step and stumbled. Two flags fluttered to the ground. His ears went hot. Everyone saw, he thought. The whole school. They'll call me Flag Boy till Class 10.
After the anthem he hid behind the water cooler.
Bhavna found him there, rubbing her cold hands. "Did my speech sound okay? I forgot one line and I think everyone noticed."
"What? No," Lokesh said. "I didn't hear any mistake."
"Good. Why are you hiding?"
"Because I fell."
Bhavna frowned. "When?"

qa.q: What did Lokesh drop when he stumbled?
qa.a: Two flags fluttered to the ground from the tray of paper flags.

qa.q: What was Lokesh worried about after he stumbled?
qa.a: Lokesh was embarrassed and scared that the whole school saw and would call him Flag Boy for years.

qa.q: What could Lokesh remind himself the next time he slips in front of people?
qa.a: Lokesh could remember that Bhavna, busy worrying about her own line, never even saw the fall, so most people are thinking about themselves.

qa.q: How did Bhavna experience the same assembly?
qa.a: Bhavna spent it worrying about her own forgotten line, so the stumble in the fog passed completely unnoticed.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles on stage believing the whole school saw, while a classmate was busy with her own worry.

passage:
On the last day before the Diwali holidays, Ma'am asked Vaibhav what seven eights were.
"Fifty-four," he said, and three people giggled.
Vaibhav spent the rest of the day with his head down. He was sure the whole class would talk about it through the holidays. On the bus he pictured them at their Diwali parties: remember Fifty-Four?
Four days later, the colony lit diyas along the compound wall. Divyansh from his class ran up with a sparkler in each hand.
"Come, my uncle got the big chakri!"
Vaibhav waited for the joke. It didn't come. Divyansh was talking about crackers, a new cycle and a cousin visiting from Pune.
"Do you remember the maths thing?" Vaibhav asked at last.
"What maths thing?" Divyansh said, already running off.

qa.q: What answer did Vaibhav give for seven eights?
qa.a: Vaibhav said fifty-four.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav worried about during the holidays?
qa.a: Vaibhav was anxious that the whole class would joke about 'Fifty-Four' at their Diwali parties.

qa.q: What might help Vaibhav feel better sooner after a wrong answer?
qa.a: Vaibhav could check the fear against reality early, maybe by asking a friend, instead of spending four days picturing the class laughing.

qa.q: What was the maths answer like for Divyansh?
qa.a: For Divyansh it was forgettable; the holidays were full of crackers, a new cycle and a cousin, so the slip had already vanished.

grounding: Shows a child who gives a wrong answer believing the class will remember it, while a classmate has forgotten it entirely.

passage:
"I'm not going to school tomorrow," Imran announced at iftar, pushing a date around his plate.
"Why?" Sabina asked.
"I forgot the third verse in poem recitation. I just stood there. Everyone was looking."
"Everyone?"
"Everyone. Thirty-two people."
Sabina tore a piece of roti. "Okay. Who forgot something in recitation last week?"
Imran frowned. "I don't know."
"Who dropped their tiffin on Monday?"
"Someone did. I don't remember who."
"So you watched thirty-two people for a whole week and remember nothing," Sabina said. "What do you think they remember about you?"
Imran was quiet. Then: "The boy next to me was yawning the whole time."
"See? One of your thirty-two was half asleep."
Imran picked up the date and ate it.

qa.q: How many people did Imran say were looking?
qa.a: Imran said thirty-two people were looking.

qa.q: Why did Imran want to skip school tomorrow?
qa.a: Imran felt embarrassed and sure that everyone had watched him forget the third verse and would remember it.

qa.q: Which question from Sabina helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking who dropped a tiffin on Monday helped, because Imran couldn't remember others' slips, so they likely wouldn't remember his.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Imran's plan to stay home?
qa.a: Sabina sees the fear as bigger than the facts and gently tests it with questions instead of laughing at it.

grounding: Shows a child who forgot a verse believing the whole class watched and will remember, until he notices how little he recalls of others' slips.

passage: At our school's Pongal celebration, I had to carry the pot of sweet pongal up to the stage. On the second step my slipper caught and I stumbled. The pot didn't fall, but I was sure the whole school saw. My face burned all through the kolam competition. That night I couldn't sleep. Everyone will call me "Stumble Keerthana" forever, I thought. The next morning I asked Sonali, "Did you see me fall yesterday?" She blinked. "You fell? I was so scared about my dance, I didn't see anything." I asked two more friends. One only remembered that the pongal tasted good. The other had spent the whole time looking for a lost earring. Nobody remembered the stumble at all.

qa.q: What was Keerthana carrying to the stage?
qa.a: The pot of sweet pongal.

qa.q: What was Keerthana worried about that night?
qa.a: Keerthana felt anxious and embarrassed, sure the whole school saw the stumble and would say "Stumble Keerthana" forever.

qa.q: What could Keerthana remember the next time something embarrassing happens?
qa.a: That most people are busy with their own worries, like Sonali's dance and the lost earring, and that checking with a friend can calm the fear.

qa.q: What was Sonali thinking about during the celebration?
qa.a: Sonali was busy being scared about the dance, so she didn't even notice the stumble.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles at a school event believing everyone saw and will remember, while the others were busy with their own worries.
